newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says crisis talks with rebels moving forward.
newsitem.headline: Peru says crisis talks with rebels moving forward.

text.p: Peru's government said on Monday arduous behind-the-scenes negotiations with Marxist rebels holding 72 captives were moving toward a bloodless solution to the 125-day hostage crisis.

"The development of the conversations, I would say, is well on track and well advanced," government negotiator Domingo Palermo said in rare public comments on the crisis. "What we are all committed to is the search for a solution to the problem, which we hope -- we are sure -- will be peaceful and as quickly as possible."
Palermo, who last met face-to-face with Tupac Amaru rebel negotiators on March 12, is holding backdoor negotiations via a three-man guarantors' commission. He did not explain his optimism.
Polls show the vast majority of Peruvians believe the four-month impasse -- stuck on the rebels' demand for the release of jailed comrades -- is set to drag on much longer.

Palermo denied last week's expulsion of a senior official of the Red Cross, which attends the hostages and is represented on the guarantors' body, or the rebels' threat over the weekend to reduce medical checkups from daily to weekly would hinder talks.

He said Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa's stated intention to limit doctors' visits "shouldn't be anything more than talk ... I hope it is not fulfilled and that attitudes of this nature are not taken because they do not contribute to a solution."

Red Cross workers were thoroughly searched by police as they entered the besieged Japanese ambassador's home Monday to carry out routine humanitarian work. Although trying to play down the expulsion, the Red Cross is calling for a full explanation from the government.

In a speech earlier on Monday, President Alberto Fujimori took a less diplomatic line than his negotiator, branding the rebels "terrorists" responsible for a dark age of violence from which Peru is only just emerging.

"We reject all forms of terrorism, from wherever it comes. No terrorist helps the image of Peru that we are creating, that of a country starting to reconstruct itself and modernise itself," he said in a speech to military officials.

Fujimori also sent a defiant message to political opponents exulting in his falling popularity and accusing his government of internal crisis and rights abuses. He said there was a campaign of "defamation" that sought "to turn criticism into a weapon ... to tie the government's hands."

Tensions ran high in Lima after two small bombs exploded at two post offices in poor districts of Lima, causing minor damage but no injuries. A third bomb, with a sign urging "popular war" and the hammer-and-sickle symbol of Peru's largest guerrilla movement, the Shining Path, was deactivated at another post office.
Shining Path has been largely overshadowed since the Dec. 17 takeover of the Japanese embassy residence by its smaller rival, the MRTA.
